title: Cloud Cost Fundamentals
summary: The pricing vocabulary and visibility practices every cost conversation starts from — before you can optimize a bill, you have to be able to read and attribute it.

slides.markdown:
Cloud cost engineering is a different discipline from on-prem budgeting: a cloud bill is a **lagging indicator** of architecture decisions made weeks earlier, not a lever you pull directly. Every unattached disk, oversized instance, and unrestricted API call is billed the moment it exists.

- The bill reflects choices made **upstream**, not last-minute negotiation.
- Fixing cost means fixing **usage and design**, not haggling for a discount.
- **Visibility** — who spent what, on what — always comes before optimization.

Providers price the same compute differently depending on how much certainty you give up.

| Model | Commitment | Discount | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| On-demand | None | 0% | Spiky workloads |
| Reserved | 1-3 years | 30-70% | Steady baseline |
| Savings plans | $/hr spend | 20-65% | Baseline that shifts |
| Spot | None — reclaimable | Up to 90% | Fault-tolerant batch |

**How to decide:** commit only what your baseline needs; cover bursts with on-demand or spot, never the reverse.

Most surprise bills trace back to a small set of repeat offenders, not exotic new services.

- **Idle resources** — a dev environment left running over a weekend, an unattached disk nobody deleted after terminating its VM.
- **Data egress** — moving data *out* of a cloud (to the internet, or across regions) is billed per GB and adds up fast; ingress is usually free.
- **Over-provisioning** — sizing for a peak that happens twice a year, then paying for that peak 24/7.

None of these shows up as one big line item — they're a thousand small ones, which is exactly why they hide.

slides.subTitle: Tagging spend to a team
slides.markdown:
You can't manage what you can't attribute. **Tagging** — key-value labels like `team:checkout` or `env:prod` attached to every resource — is what turns one undifferentiated bill into a spend-per-team, spend-per-product breakdown.

Without tags, the bill is a single number nobody can act on. With tags, a cost report answers "why did we spend $40k more this month" in minutes instead of a week of guessing, because every resource already declares who owns it.

Both make spend visible, but only one makes it hurt.

| | Showback | Chargeback |
|---|---|---|
| What happens | Team sees its own cost report | Team's budget is actually billed |
| Enforcement | Social pressure, awareness | Real budget impact |
| Typical use | Early-stage cost culture | Mature orgs with per-team P&L |

**How to decide:** start with showback — chargeback without accurate tagging first just produces disputes about whose resource something actually was.

slides.subTitle: Reading a cost breakdown
slides.markdown:
A team's bill is $12,000 over last month's baseline. The breakdown by tag shows: compute +$1,200, storage +$800, **data transfer +$9,400**.

The instinct is to hunt for a runaway VM — but the dominant line item is egress. Tracing further: a new nightly job started replicating a full dataset to a partner's cloud account in another region, at cents per GB across terabytes. The fix isn't rightsizing a server; it's transferring only the delta, or co-locating the partner's read access in-region.

slides.subTitle: No tagging strategy
slides.markdown:
The wrong belief: "we'll tag things properly once cost becomes a problem." By the time cost is a problem, hundreds of untagged resources already exist, and retrofitting tags means chasing every team to ask "is this yours, and why does it exist."

The correct model: tagging is enforced at resource-**creation** time — via IaC policy or a provisioning gate that rejects untagged resources — not applied retroactively. An org that tags from day one can explain nearly all of its bill; one that doesn't usually can't explain half of it.
